title: Home Inspections in Texas: What Buyers Should Know
summary: Learn how home inspections work in Texas, including TREC standards, soil and foundation checks, specialized add-ons, and phase inspections for new builds.

Posted by[Patrick Begg](https://www.mihomes.com/blog/patrick-begg) in[Home Buying](https://www.mihomes.com/blog/home-buying)


)


A **Texas home inspection** is an independent evaluation of a home's structural integrity, mechanical systems, and safety features. Performed by a licensed inspector using state-standardized TREC forms, it identifies physical deficiencies before closing.


Buying a home is one of the most significant investments you will ever make. Whether you are purchasing a resale property or exploring[new homes in Texas](https://www.mihomes.com/new-homes/texas) , a comprehensive home inspection provides clarity and leverage to protect your investment. In Texas, specific climate factors, unique pest risks, and state-mandated inspection guidelines make understanding this process essential for every homebuyer.


From evaluating foundation performance on expansive clay soils to navigating phase inspections on new builds, here is what you need to know about home inspections in Texas.


## How Do Home Inspections Work in Texas?


Home inspections in Texas operate under a unique regulatory framework governed by state law. Unlike states with varied reporting standards, Texas streamlines the process so buyers know exactly what to expect from their inspection report.


Regulatory Component Texas Standard Why It Matters to Buyers


**Licensing Authority**[Texas Real Estate Commission (TREC)](https://www.trec.texas.gov/) Inspectors must complete rigorous state education, background checks, and proctored licensing exams.


**Standardized Reporting** TREC Form REI 7-6 (Property Inspection Report) Provides a consistent, easy-to-read layout across all residential property evaluations in Texas.


**Evaluation Standard** "Deficient" Notation Properties do not "pass" or "fail"; inspectors mark specific systems that are not performing as intended or are unsafe.


**Contract Timing** Build Milestones / Phase Inspections Gives buyers dedicated windows to evaluate framing, mechanical rough-ins, and final operational features.


## 4 Texas Climate and Structural Focus Areas


The Texas environment presents distinct challenges for residential construction. According to building science research from the[Texas Real Estate Research Center at Texas A&M University](https://trerc.tamu.edu/) , local climate conditions require home inspectors to pay specialized attention to four structural vulnerabilities:


### 1. Soil and Foundation Performance


Much of Texas features highly expansive clay soil, which expands significantly when wet and contracts during hot, dry weather. This constant movement puts immense strain on concrete slab and pier-and-beam foundations. Inspectors examine interior drywall for stress cracks, check window and door frame alignment, and evaluate site drainage to detect early foundation movement.


### 2. HVAC and Attic Insulation Under Extreme Heat


With summers bringing extended stretches of triple-digit weather, efficient air conditioning is a necessity. Citing thermal comfort data from the[National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA)](https://www.noaa.gov/) , inspectors test cooling performance differentials (temperature drop across supply and return ducts), verify attic ductwork insulation seals, and ensure ventilation meets current energy efficiency benchmarks.


### 3. Roof Systems and Storm Exposure


From severe hail and high winds to intense ultraviolet exposure, Texas roofs endure severe weather strain. Inspectors evaluate shingle condition, flashing around chimneys and roof valleys, roof decking integrity, and gutter capacity to catch minor vulnerabilities before they cause internal water damage.


### 4. Site Grading and Drainage


Torrential rains and sudden severe weather mean water management around the foundation is critical. Inspectors verify that site soil slopes away from the home (a minimum slope drop over the first six feet) and ensure downspouts divert runoff water away from the foundation perimeter.


## Essential Specialized Add-On Inspections in Texas


While a standard TREC inspection covers primary structural and mechanical systems, Texas environmental conditions often call for specialized testing:


- **Wood-Destroying Insect (WDI) Inspection:** Termites and carpenter ants thrive in warm Texas climates. Note that TREC licensing does not cover pest inspection; inspectors must be separately licensed by the[Texas Department of Agriculture (TDA)](https://www.texasagriculture.gov/) to issue an official WDI report.
- **Sewer Scope Camera Inspection:** Expansive clay soils can shift underground drain lines, leading to bellies, cracks, or offsets in plumbing lines. A sewer scope camera evaluates the main waste line from the home to the municipal sewer tie-in or septic system.
- **Pool and Spa Inspection:** For homes featuring in-ground pools, inspectors evaluate pump operation, filter pressure, heater elements, and safety barrier compliance per local municipal codes.


## New Construction Inspection Stages


While municipal city inspectors verify minimum building code compliance on new builds, buyers have built-in peace of mind through structured quality milestones—including pre-drywall reviews, blue tape walkthroughs, and final orientations alongside their construction team. For buyers who choose to hire a third-party inspector to complement these steps, independent evaluations typically align across three key milestones:


- **Pre-Drywall Inspection:** Conducted right after framing, roof installation, electrical wiring, plumbing rough-ins, and HVAC ductwork are complete, but before insulation and drywall cover the internal walls. This allows inspectors to identify structural framing issues, pinched wiring, or improperly routed pipes while they remain visible.
- **Final Pre-Closing Inspection:** Completed roughly one to two weeks before your final buyer orientation. The independent inspector verifies that all mechanical systems function properly, major appliances operate correctly, and[construction quality standards](https://www.mihomes.com/why-mi/quality) are fully met.
- **11-Month Warranty Inspection:** Scheduled shortly before your initial one-year builder warranty expires. This inspection identifies subtle items that may have developed during the home's first seasonal cycle, aligning with standard 1-Year Workmanship, 2-Year Mechanical, and 10-Year Structural warranty protection plans.


If you choose to hire an independent inspector during your build, your New Home Consultant can provide specific timing guidance and coordinate jobsite access details with your construction team.


## How Buyers Should Use Their Inspection Findings


Receiving an inspection report that is 40 to 60 pages long can feel overwhelming. Consumer advice guidelines from the[U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD)](https://www.hud.gov/) recommend keeping a clear perspective on how to interpret the results:


- **Focus on Major Systems:** Distinguish between primary structural or safety concerns (such as electrical hazards, roof leaks, or foundation failure) and minor cosmetic items like scuffed baseboards or loose cabinet handles.
- **Coordinate Timing Early:** On new construction builds, align inspection dates with your construction schedule so any verified findings can be reviewed prior to your final orientation.
- **Keep Communication Factual:** Use the standardized TREC report findings as an objective reference to coordinate directly with your builder on essential safety and functional items.


### Pro Tip


If your independent inspector identifies legitimate code, safety, or operational items during a pre-closing inspection, share the complete report directly with your New Home Consultant. Established builder quality standards and structural warranty guidelines ensure valid functional deficiencies are addressed prior to closing.


To see how quality inspections fit into the broader roadmap of building and closing on a new home, explore our complete guide to the[steps to build a home](https://www.mihomes.com/blog/what-are-the-steps-to-build-a-home) .


## Navigating Your Texas Home Inspection with Confidence


Confidence in your new home starts with knowing it’s built with care. With M/I Homes, your construction team provides dedicated oversight, detailed quality checks, and final walkthroughs throughout the building process. You’ll also stay connected with and be able to communicate directly to your construction manager through our[Journey app](https://www.mihomes.com/why-mi/journey) , with updates as your home comes together. While we stand behind the quality of every home we build, you’re always welcome to hire an independent inspector if you’d like an additional level of assurance.


## Frequently Asked Questions About Texas Home Inspections


### Are home inspections mandatory in Texas?


Home inspections are not legally required by the state of Texas, but they are strongly recommended by real estate professionals and consumer advocacy agencies. Most mortgage lenders also require specialized appraisals or structural certifications before funding a loan.


### How much does a typical home inspection cost in Texas?


Depending on square footage, property age, and local market (e.g., Dallas-Fort Worth, Austin, Houston, or San Antonio), a standard residential TREC inspection generally ranges from $350 to $650+. Specialized testing—such as TDA termite (WDI) reports ($100–$200) or sewer scope camera tests ($250–$400)—involves separate fees.


### What is a TREC Form REI 7-6?


[TREC Form REI 7-6 (Property Inspection Report)](https://www.trec.texas.gov/forms/property-inspection-report) is the official document mandated by the Texas Real Estate Commission. It establishes standard criteria for evaluating structural systems, electrical wiring, heating and cooling equipment, plumbing, appliances, and optional systems like irrigation or swimming pools.
